title: Valid Parentheses
description: Brute force to optimized: repeatedly erasing matched pairs versus a single-pass stack that checks each closing bracket against the current top.

blocks.text: Given a string s containing just the characters '(', ')', '{', '}', '[', and ']', determine if the input string is valid. A string is valid if: every opening bracket is closed by the same TYPE of closing bracket, and opening brackets are closed in the CORRECT ORDER (the most recently opened one must be closed first).

blocks.caption: A stack tracks unmatched opening brackets; each closing bracket must match whatever is currently on TOP of the stack

blocks.text: Every closing bracket must correspond to the MOST RECENTLY opened, still-unclosed bracket of the matching type; if any closing bracket does not match what was most recently opened, or if the string ends with unmatched opening brackets remaining, the string is invalid.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Stack of Nested Boxes That Must Be Closed in Reverse Order
blocks.text: Imagine opening a series of nested boxes, one inside another. To validly close them all back up, the innermost (most recently opened) box must always be closed FIRST, before any box that contains it. Trying to close an outer box while an inner one is still open is invalid, exactly like a mismatched bracket sequence.

blocks.caption: Push every opening bracket; on a closing bracket, pop and verify it matches the expected type

blocks.text: Before repeatedly scanning and erasing matched pairs from the string (slow and clumsy), notice that a stack directly models "the most recently opened bracket must close first," resolving both type and order in a single pass.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Every opening bracket needs to be "remembered" until its matching closing bracket is found.

Observation 2: The bracket that must be closed NEXT is always the MOST RECENTLY opened one still unmatched, exactly the last-in-first-out behavior a stack provides.

Observation 3: On each closing bracket, popping the stack's top and checking it matches the expected opening type directly verifies both the type AND the order in one step.

Observation 4: If a closing bracket appears when the stack is empty (nothing to match against), or the popped bracket does not match, the string is immediately invalid.

Observation 5: After processing the entire string, the stack must be completely empty for the string to be valid: any remaining unmatched opening brackets mean the string was never properly closed.
This is the classic stack-based bracket matching technique: push every opening bracket, and on each closing bracket, verify it matches whatever is currently on top of the stack.
Repeatedly search for and remove any innermost matched pair ("()", "[]", or "{}") from the string, until no more such pairs exist; the string is valid only if it becomes completely empty.

items: Search the string for any occurrence of "()", "[]", or "{}" and remove it.
Repeat until no more such pairs can be found; the string is valid if and only if it is now completely empty.

codes.python:
def is_valid(s):
    while '()' in s or '[]' in s or '{}' in s:                             # repeatedly erase any innermost matched pair
        s = s.replace('()', '').replace('[]', '').replace('{}', '')
    return s == ''                                                          # valid only if EVERYTHING cancels out completely


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(is_valid("()[]{}"))
    print(is_valid("([)]"))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Repeatedly removing any innermost matched pair simulates "resolving" brackets from the inside out, eventually reducing a valid string to nothing.
This directly reflects the definition of validity, but does so very inefficiently, rescanning the string from scratch after every single removal.

blocks.text: Correctly determines validity, since repeatedly removing matched innermost pairs is a valid (if slow) way to fully resolve a properly nested string down to nothing.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n^2) in the worst case, since each removal can require rescanning the string from scratch.
Space: O(n), for the string being repeatedly modified.
Limitation: repeatedly rescanning the string is far slower than necessary; a stack resolves the exact same logic in a single O(n) pass.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force repeatedly rescans the whole string after each removal. Instead, use a stack: push every opening bracket as it is encountered. On a closing bracket, immediately check whether the stack's top matches the expected type (popping it if so); if not (or the stack is empty), the string is invalid immediately. At the end, the string is valid only if the stack is completely empty.

Walk through the string once. For each opening bracket, push it. For each closing bracket, check if the stack is empty or its top does not match the expected corresponding opening bracket; if so, return false immediately. After the full walk, return whether the stack is empty.
Push opening brackets onto a stack; verify each closing bracket against the stack's current top in a single linear pass.

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: The function returns false as soon as the mismatch is detected, matching the expected result.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass through the string.
Space: O(n), for the stack in the worst case (all opening brackets).

The stack always holds exactly the sequence of currently unmatched opening brackets, from oldest (bottom) to most recent (top). Since a valid string requires the MOST RECENTLY opened bracket to close FIRST, checking each closing bracket against the stack's top is precisely the correct check. If the string is valid throughout and the stack ends up empty, every opening bracket found its match in the correct order.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["A closing bracket matches the stack's top","Pop it and continue"],["A closing bracket does NOT match the top (or the stack is empty)","Immediately invalid, return false"],["The string ends with the stack still non-empty","Invalid: some opening brackets were never closed"]]}

items: A hash map from each closing bracket to its expected opening match keeps the comparison logic clean and easy to extend to more bracket types.
Checking "stack is empty" BEFORE popping prevents an error when a closing bracket appears with no corresponding opening bracket at all.
The final "stack is empty" check catches the case of unmatched opening brackets remaining at the end (e.g., the string "(((").

blocks.text: Whenever a "must close/resolve in reverse order of opening" structure appears (brackets, nested scopes, matching tags), a stack is almost always the right tool, since it naturally provides last-in-first-out access matching that exact requirement.

items: Forgetting to check whether the stack is empty before popping on a closing bracket, causing an error on strings like just ")".
Forgetting the final "is the stack empty" check, incorrectly accepting strings with leftover unmatched opening brackets like "(((".
Comparing bracket CHARACTERS directly instead of using a proper type-matching map, which can get error-prone with more bracket types.

items: Explicitly stating "a stack models last-in-first-out, exactly matching how nested brackets must resolve" up front demonstrates the key pattern-recognition insight clearly.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Brackets/parentheses must close in the correct NESTED order" points directly toward a stack-based matching approach.

items: How would you extend this to also validate custom bracket-like tags (e.g., HTML tags)? The exact same stack technique applies, pushing opening tags and matching them against closing tags.
What is the maximum stack size needed, and when does it occur? Up to n/2 in the worst case, when the first half of the string consists entirely of opening brackets.

How would you modify this to also RETURN the position of the first invalid character, rather than just true/false? Track the current index when a mismatch or empty-stack pop is detected, and return that index instead of immediately returning false.
The foundational stack-based matching pattern that generalizes to many other problems in this category, including Longest Valid Parentheses and Score of Parentheses.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n^2) time, O(n) space.
Optimized (stack-based single pass): O(n) time, O(n) space.

items: Pattern: Stack-based bracket matching
Core Idea: Push opening brackets; on each closing bracket, verify it matches the stack's current top, popping it; the string is valid only if the stack ends empty
Time: O(n)
Space: O(n)
Most Important Observation: A stack's last-in-first-out behavior exactly matches the requirement that the most recently opened bracket must close first
Interview Difficulty: Easy
One-line memory trick: Push opens; on a close, pop and check it matches; valid only if the stack ends empty
